Engineering Principles

This document records the reusable engineering principles behind Builder Garage and how mature each one is. It adds no requirements.

What Builder Garage requires is defined by the canonical skills, the responsibility floor and extension-point registry, GOVERNANCE.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, the architectural direction, and accepted ADRs. Where this document and one of those sources differ, the source is authoritative.

The principles come from engineering practice described in history.md.

Status

Status Meaning
Established Already required. Listed here with a link to the source that requires it, and not restated.
Candidate Supported by concrete engineering evidence. Not required. Reviewers and contributors may use it as a judgment aid. Not following an unapproved candidate is not, by itself, a blocking finding. An actual defect found by applying a candidate is still judged under the established review contract, like any other defect.
Hypothesis Supported by experience, not yet resolved.
Open question Tracked as a GitHub issue.

A candidate becomes a requirement only through the normal contribution process: an issue, independent review, and maintainer approval, with the requirement written into the canonical skill or governance document that owns it. Appearing here does not make anything a requirement.

Principle Required by
Make engineering expectations explicit instead of relying on memory or convention. Durable artifacts carry context: the Issue/PR holds what, the skill holds how, and the prompt holds action and location. README: Operating model, CONTRIBUTING: Changing skills and standards
Understand a non-trivial change before implementing it. implementation-readiness-workflow, engineering-discovery-workflow
The implementer never approves their own work. Independent review happens before the change is proposed as a pull request, so the pull request is not the first serious review. GOVERNANCE: Review requirements, independent-implementation-review
Corrections do not restore approval. Only independent re-review does. GOVERNANCE: Review requirements, application-implementation-workflow
Correct the demonstrated cause, not only the reported permutation, within the issue's scope. application-implementation-workflow: Coherent correction boundary

Candidates

Evidence and verification

  • Evidence-bounded claims. A validation artifact supports only claims within what it can observe. Compilation, source inspection, tests, generated artifacts, independent review, integration behavior, and physical-device testing establish different kinds of evidence. "Verified", "not verified", and "not verifiable at this layer" are all legitimate results. Absence of evidence is not proof.
  • Layer-appropriate verification. Verify a behavior at the boundary that can observe it. Repository logic, generated artifacts, browser integration, external services, and physical devices may each need a different method.
  • Mechanism-specific source verification. A source supports a claim only when it supports the exact mechanism claimed, not an adjacent topic. For a material claim about agent or tool behavior: state the precise causal claim, identify the system boundary, obtain the exact supporting quotation or primary documentation, compare it with the claim, and record remaining uncertainty. In particular, a generated explanation that would shape an engineering workflow or policy needs direct supporting evidence before it is codified.
  • Regression sensitivity. For an important invariant or a previously found defect class, confirm when practical that violating the invariant makes the expected tests fail. A passing test alone does not show that it would catch the regression. Recognition cues (non-binding): the change protects an important invariant, or corrects a defect class that has been found before. It is not meant to apply automatically to trivial changes. These cues are judgment aids only; see Recognition cues.

Authority

  • Explicit authority and precedence. When two values must always agree, first ask whether both should exist. A concern should have one authoritative representation at a given level, with other representations derived from it. A system may still hold several kinds of truth, such as product intent, configuration, runtime state, observations, and inferences. Each should have an identifiable authority and an explicit precedence over competing representations.
  • Capability does not imply authority. An actor, component, or model able to perform an operation is not thereby authorized to decide what that operation represents.
  • Boundaries should not silently weaken semantics. Crossing an API, persistence, transport, lifecycle, or asynchronous boundary should preserve the behavior the system depends on, even where a weaker implementation appears to work.

Stateful and asynchronous systems

These apply only where a change owns state, asynchronous work, a UI lifecycle, or an external resource. They do not widen the review boundaries the canonical skills define. Each carries non-binding recognition cues; see Recognition cues.

  • Review state machines, not only happy paths. Review a stateful or asynchronous feature across its meaningful transitions, terminal paths, failure paths, and stale-event behavior, as well as its nominal journey. Derive the relevant scenarios from the feature itself, not from a universal checklist. The canonical skills already require a bounded form of this, but only when a demonstrated defect exposes a shared rule; see Established. The broader up-front form is a candidate only. Recognition cues (non-binding): the change adds or alters a feature with distinct states and transitions, such as a session or a multi-step flow, or it handles failure, cancellation, retry, repetition, re-entry, replacement, or events that can arrive late.
  • Timing is part of correctness. An invariant has a time by which it must hold, whether event-synchronous, commit-synchronous, before observation or paint, or eventual. Eventually holding is not always enough. Recognition cues (non-binding): an invariant must hold by a particular point, such as before an event handler returns, at commit, or before the user can observe the result, in a UI lifecycle, streaming, or other time-sensitive path.
  • Revoke authority before unreliable cleanup. Withdraw logical authority before calling cleanup that may throw, re-enter, call back later, or fail to release the resource. Recognition cues (non-binding): the change acquires or releases an externally controlled resource, such as a subscription, stream, worker, socket, observer, timer, or SDK session.
  • Stale work is powerless. Results from terminated, superseded, canceled, or unauthorized work must not change current authoritative state. Recognition cues (non-binding): asynchronous or session-oriented work can be terminated, superseded, or canceled while its results are still pending.
  • Separate state domains. Application state, external lifecycle state such as browser or SDK state, and physical resource state are distinct. Evidence about one does not establish another. Recognition cues (non-binding): the change involves a browser, device, platform, hardware, distributed, or otherwise externally owned resource.
  • Do not regress an authoritatively accepted value. Once the application has accepted or displayed a value as current, a later external reconciliation should not silently replace it merely because the external system defines finality more narrowly. Recognition cues (non-binding): the change handles streaming, optimistic, user-input, or asynchronous reconciliation workflows.

Recognition cues

The recognition cues beside the conditional candidates above are judgment aids, drawn from the conditional notes on items 11–16 and 18 of the retired initial inventory, whose disposition is recorded in history.md. They impose no trigger, gate, or requirement. A change that matches a cue is not thereby required to apply the candidate, and not applying it is not, by itself, a blocking finding. If a candidate is later promoted, its requirement and its trigger are added together in the canonical skill that owns them (#7 decision, item 7).

Product surface

  • Keep agent collaboration context out of customer UI. Agent-readable context belongs in non-customer channels: repository structure, component names, comments, structured metadata, project instructions, test identifiers, and authorized tool context. Rendering a string in the UI gives an agent no memory it lacks from source access. Before release, review visible strings, labels, badges, tooltips, empty and error states, controls, and diagnostics in customer-representative states. Use automated scans to surface candidates, then make a human product judgment. Preserve accessibility labels, customer-relevant status, useful diagnostics, and intended error handling. Product-intent acceptance more broadly is decided: an explicit human authority accepts product intent, not an agent or an agent gate, and inspects a user-facing result in the form a user meets it when that is practical (#8 decision, items 1 and 3; F12, E8, E9, GOVERNANCE: Product-intent acceptance).

Lifecycle and method

  • Progressive uncertainty reduction. Each stage should narrow the kinds of surprise left for the next, so that promotion confirms rather than discovers.
  • Progressive formalization. Practices move from observed experience to an articulated principle, to a standard, and to enforcement only where that is warranted. A standard should be justified by engineering need, and not everything needs to become executable.
  • Adopt your own framework visibly. A framework publisher adopts its own artifacts through the same visible mechanisms any adopting project would use, and records its project deltas. It treats its self-use as single-project evidence, not as proof of general suitability. Self-use can surface friction and demonstrate one adoption; it cannot show that the framework suits other projects. This candidate creates no review gate and requires no claim about downstream adopters. Builder Garage's own adoption records are its skill-adoption profile and Go Manual profile, and friction is recorded in Application Improvement Suggestions (#22 decision, item 6).

Hypotheses

  • Comprehension debt. Agent-assisted construction can outpace the understanding of the people accountable for the software. Preserving reasoning, decisions, and trade-offs may be an engineering property, not only documentation.
  • Intentional compromise. Technical debt and temporary limitations can be legitimate when chosen and bounded deliberately. The distinction that matters is deliberate compromise versus degradation discovered later.
  • Invariants and context-sensitive expressions. A small set of obligations might hold everywhere while projects satisfy them through different mechanisms. Builder Garage has since taken this shape: the #7 decision assigned the obligations no configuration may weaken to a responsibility floor (item 2), now F1–F14, and projects make their own choices at the declared extension points of the extension-point registry (#16 decision). Whether that shape suits projects in general is still a hypothesis.
  • The framework governs how project truth is established, not the truth itself. Builder Garage has since taken this direction: Garage defines contracts and validates configuration and the structure of evidence, while each project supplies its own values within the responsibility floor (#6 direction, items 3 and 8; #16 decision, configuration model). Whether the distinction holds in general is still a hypothesis.

Open questions

None is currently open. The discovery-era questions, #6, #7, and #8, were closed with maintainer decisions. Their outcomes are recorded in history.md and in the sections above.

New open questions are tracked as GitHub issues, for example a discovery issue, and are listed here while they remain open.
